extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalists, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for understanding how individual images of the world ('pseudo-environments'), censorship, media, and social conditions shape public opinion and the circulation of ideas. Emphasizes limits on access to facts, propaganda techniques, and the need for expert organization of unseen facts for representative decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment as determinant of behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that what each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him; 'The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if an atlas says the world is flat, a sailor will avoid the edge; if maps include a fountain of youth, explorers will seek it; if yellow dirt looks like gold, people will act as if it is gold. Propaganda substitutes one social pattern for another by altering these pictures (e.g., class consciousness, national consciousness). The pseudo-environment determines effort, feelings, hopes, not necessarily accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on access to facts (chief factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate the chief external factors that limit people's access to the facts about public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lays out the principal limiting factors to be examined: 'the artificial censorships, the limitations of social contact, the comparatively meager time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs, the distortion arising because events have to be compressed into very short messages, the difficulty of making a small vocabulary express a complicated world, and finally the fear of facing those facts which would seem to threaten the established routine of men's lives.' Use these as explicit categories when diagnosing why public knowledge diverges from reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial censorships as enablers of propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship (a barrier between public and event), propaganda in the strict sense is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship limits access to the real environment, allowing actors to 'decide where [people] shall look, and at what.' Military censorship is an obvious form, but the concept extends to legal powers, control of correspondents, wires, passports, and secret services. Evaluate presence and effects of such barriers when assessing possible manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of social contact and circulation channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Social segregation, grooves, enclaves, and limited social contact narrow who hears about what and how quickly information spreads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider travel, trade, mails, wires, radio, roads, and transport infrastructure as determinants of idea circulation. Use wartime mobilization (Creel's campaign) as a benchmark for how much effort is required to reach 'everybody'; in peace-time such reach is rare, leaving whole groups only vaguely informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited attention/time available for public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparatively meager time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs constrains the public's ability to form informed opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public knowledge, account for attention scarcity; extensive propaganda campaigns (e.g., Four Minute Men, distribution of materials) are required to overcome this constraint. Recognize that normal channels in peacetime do not supply the same intensity of exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and distortion from short messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Events often must be compressed into very short messages, causing distortion and the loss of nuance necessary to understand complex affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how compression (headlines, brief communiqués, short news items) shapes mental pictures. Example: wartime communiqués that omitted context produced misleading impressions of battles (Verdun examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small vocabulary versus complex world
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited public vocabulary makes it difficult to express and communicate complex realities accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how lexical constraints and repeated formulae ('under our artillery and machine gun fire', 'mowed down by our artillery') simplify and frame events, reinforcing specific inferences by repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of facing facts that threaten routines
rubrics_metrics.description: People and institutions may avoid confronting facts that threaten established routines or comfortable beliefs, skewing public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing opinions, check for systematic omission of threatening facts (e.g., omission of home casualties while emphasizing enemy losses) and consider psychological resistance to disruptive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceptions and stored images shaping perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Stored images, preconceptions, and prejudices interpret incoming messages and powerfully direct attention and vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the internal filters (stereotypes, stored images) that fill out scant messages and determine what elements are noticed or ignored. Use psychoanalytic insights (dreams, fantasy, rationalization) to understand formation of these internal representations, but do not assume the analyst's criterion of a 'normal biological career' applies to sociological analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallization of individual opinions into Public Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how individual pictures and interests become identified with groups and how they crystallize into Public Opinion, a National Will, Group Mind, or Social Purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study processes (communication, organization, leadership, institutional channels) through which dispersed private opinions cohere into collective opinions acted upon by groups or in the name of groups. The text promises subsequent chapters examining these crystallization mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of propaganda: selection, omission, repetition, framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda operates by selecting which facts to present, omitting others, repeating certain images or figures, and framing events to induce particular inferences without formal argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by French General Staff practices at Verdun: emphasizing enemy losses, omitting French casualties, repeating casualty statistics, and framing communiqués to produce reassurance or particular strategic impressions. When evaluating messages, identify these techniques and their intended inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of information control used by authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities control selection of correspondents, their movements, censorship of dispatches, operation of wires, and leverage government powers (cables, passports, mails, customs, blockades) to influence what the public perceives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional capacity to control news (military staff, ministries, diplomatic/civil censorship), and note differential control across domains (armies less controllable than navies/diplomacy; soldiers' talk and enemy communiqués can pierce controls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy as a shifting barrier to public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide variety of matters are treated as private to differing degrees (fortunes, salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet meetings, medical conversations), and the elasticity of what is 'private' affects public access to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing the provenance of an opinion, ask: who actually saw or counted the facts? Was it direct observation or several removals? Use historical examples (treaty secrets, investigations into life insurance, scandals published in press) to show how privacy boundaries change and affect public awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert organization to represent unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot function successfully unless personal representation is supplemented by independent, expert organizations that make unseen facts intelligible to decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that political science (expert organizations) should 'formulate, in advance of real decision,' rather than merely apologize or report after decisions are made. The press cannot be relied on to perform this task because of the nature of news and the economic basis of journalism; public opinions must be organized for the press, not by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic caution: do not take current public opinion as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The sociologist must not take the products of existing public opinion (the 'normal social career' or a career 'freed from suppressions') as the criterion by which to study public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservative critics assume an existing normal social career; romantic critics assume a liberated ideal; both take the world for granted. Sociologists must instead study how the pseudo-environment is constructed and avoid circular reasoning that uses public opinion as both subject and standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and opportunity as determinants of reach and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical reach of propaganda or information campaigns depends on the machinery, personnel, money, and channels available (e.g., releases, speakers, teachers' periodicals, lantern slides, posters, civic organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Creel's wartime mobilization (thousands of releases, tens of thousands of speakers, distribution to teachers, use of civic channels) as an empirical benchmark. Assess how much organizational effort is required to produce a uniform public opinion and recognize that such effort is usually absent in peacetime.
